comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
Not sure Software 3.0 will be big models training small models.

I mean, yes. We will see a lot of that. But i don't see it as a step change up from 2.0, as 2.0 was a step change from 1.0.

Karpathy himself warned about the diminishment of model effectiveness when overwriting, or abstracting from, model weights. If you want a better model, you retrain it with new data and old data. Get weights right for the whole enchilada.

If you abstract a smaller model from a larger one, will there be a bias towards the mean? A lesser field of competence?

I dunno.

I've been thinking instead of 3.0 as self-improving, self-actualizing, self-optimizing models. Q-Star, perhaps. A little furthur down that path is AGI.

I don't think this two-tiered model development idea is on that path. But maybe I'm wrong?

comments.author: @RasmusSchultz
comments.text:
I'm sorry, but calling it "software 2.0" or "3.0" is silly. The model itself isn't code, it's data. And LLMs are not replacing software in general. As you already know, AI is great for fuzzy problems, for which actual software doesn't work well - and it's absolutely awful for many other things, for which software works great. If you're thinking LLMs will eventually write all the software, unsupervised, I don't really see it. The issue is that LLM is unpredictable, and it's designed to be. Software is calculus, it's predictable - even when software is wrong, it's reliable, in the sense that bugs don't just come and go unless somebody changes the code.

When LLM hallucinates and gives wrong answers, we tend to think of this as a bug, but being unpredictable isn't a bug - it's a feature. Randomness and errors is built into the algorithm, by design, completely intentionally. It's not a "bug" that's going to get "fixed". Here, watch Nate Jones talking about it in this video:

https://youtu.be/ODLyBQd4VHU?si=BiDMuVdG6i4iRHO1
